pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Why circuit components behave differently

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England, KS2 Year 6 Electricity, statutory, verbatim):** 'compare and give reasons for variations in how components function, including the brightness of bulbs, the loudness of buzzers and the on/off position of switches.' Non-statutory: series only; work scientifically by systematically changing one component at a time.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NATIONAL (NGSS): no direct grade-5/6 circuit performance expectation (UK-anchored; circuit reasoning lands at MS). Sits on 'More batteries, brighter bulb' and is intuitive grounding for KS3 series-vs-parallel.

- **Operational details:** Children compare circuits and give reasons for variations in how components function: brightness of bulbs, loudness of buzzers, and the on/off effect of switch positions.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A→B (concrete, moving toward giving REASONS, age 10-11). The step up from the previous topic is EXPLANATION — not just 'more cells = brighter' but reasoning about why adding more bulbs in series dims them, why a switch position turns things on/off, why a buzzer is louder. Kept qualitative; KS2 SERIES circuits only; no Ohm's law or quantitative resistance.
bestPractices: Drive it with systematic comparison — change ONE thing at a time (number of cells, number of bulbs, a switch open/closed) and compare — so each variation's cause is isolated (the Y6 working-scientifically steer).

Separate the two opposite moves explicitly: adding CELLS increases brightness (more push), adding BULBS in series decreases each bulb's brightness (the push/energy is shared) — children must hold both.
Demand reasoned explanations, not just observations: 'the two bulbs are equally dim because the same current flows through both and the push is shared between them' — model the sentence frame.
Show series bulbs are EQUALLY bright (not brighter nearer the battery) to confront the current-used-up idea head-on — the current is the same all the way round.

Keep the qualitative reason honest: at KS2 frame it as the cells' push being shared among more components; flag that the precise reason (more components → more resistance → less current) is formalised at KS3, so loose 'energy used up' talk isn't entrenched.
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side comparison circuits: 1 bulb vs 2 bulbs in series (both dimmer, equally), 1 cell vs 2 cells (brighter).
Two equally-dim series bulbs annotated 'same current through both' to kill the nearest-is-brightest idea.
A switch shown open (off) and closed (on) as the simplest component variation.
A reason frame / sentence starter: 'This bulb is ___ because ___ (more cells push harder / the push is shared between more bulbs / the switch breaks the loop).'
commonMisconceptions: Current used up / attenuation — the bulb nearest the battery is brightest and later ones dimmer; in series all bulbs are EQUALLY bright.
Confusing adding components with adding cells — expecting 'more bulbs = brighter' when more bulbs in series makes each dimmer.
Clashing currents — explaining brightness by current meeting from both terminals.
Thinking a component's behaviour depends on its POSITION in the series loop rather than on the whole circuit.
Treating 'energy is shared/used up' too literally — useful as a KS2 reason for dimming but must not harden into 'current gets used up' (KS3 corrects this with resistance/current).

learn.summary: For ages 10–11 (UK KS2 Year 6 Electricity): children compare series circuits and give REASONS for variations in how components behave — brightness of bulbs, loudness of buzzers, and the on/off effect of switch positions. The core objective is explanation, not just observation: moving beyond 'more cells = brighter' to reasoning about why adding more bulbs in series dims each one, why a switch position breaks or completes the loop, and why a buzzer is louder with more cells. Work is driven by systematic one-change-at-a-time comparison and kept qualitative (series circuits for the main investigations, with parallel only as an optional extension prediction; no Ohm's law or quantitative resistance). The central misconception to confront is 'current used up on the way round' — the idea that the bulb nearest the battery is brightest. In a series loop the current is the same everywhere, so identical series bulbs glow equally (apart from small differences between real bulbs).

activities.title: Compare-and-reason circuit bench: add a second bulb
feedback: If the learner predicts the near bulb is brighter: show the two bulbs glowing equally, then reverse the cell to show 'first' is not a real position in the loop — the current is equal everywhere.

If the learner expects two bulbs to be brighter than one ('more bulbs = more light'): compare one bulb to two in series directly and connect the dimmer result to the push being shared, not multiplied.

If the learner explains brightness as current arriving from both battery terminals and 'clashing' at a bulb: trace the single continuous direction of flow round the loop and show the current is one flow that is the same at every point — it does not meet from two sides.
Reinforce the correct explanation: 'equal, and both dimmer than one, because the current is the same all the way round and the push is shared between the two bulbs.'
activities.rationale: The statutory aim is to compare and give reasons for component variations, changing one thing at a time. A direct add-and-compare, with a visible current trace and a prediction committed before looking, is intended to surface the 'current used up' model; the equal-dimming result then confronts it.
sourceClaims: Y6 Electricity statutory requirement (verbatim): 'compare and give reasons for variations in how components function, including the brightness of bulbs, the loudness of buzzers and the on/off position of switches'; series only; change one component at a time.
The current-used-up/attenuation model (bulb nearest battery brightest) is a dominant misconception; series bulbs are equally bright because current is the same all the way round.
learnerActions: Build or set up a series circuit with one bright bulb and one cell; observe and name its brightness.
Add a SECOND identical bulb in series. Before looking, predict whether the first bulb will stay the same, get brighter, or get dimmer, and whether the two bulbs will match.

Observe that BOTH bulbs are dimmer than the single bulb was and that the two identical bulbs glow equally (any small difference comes from the bulbs themselves, not from which one is nearer the cell).

Trace the current all the way round the loop (use a simulation's current indicator/band, or ammeters placed at different points in a real circuit) and check that it is the same through both bulbs; drawn arrows show the path but cannot measure the current.
State a reason using a sentence frame: 'This bulb is ___ because ___' (e.g. 'both bulbs are equally dim because the same current flows through both and the cell's push is shared between them').
Reverse the cell and observe that it still makes no difference which bulb is 'first'.
activities.intendedInsight: In a single series loop the current is the same through every component, so neither bulb gets 'more' first; adding a second identical bulb dims BOTH equally because the cell's push (voltage) is shared, not because current is used up along the way.

activities.title: Hold the two opposite moves together: more cells vs more bulbs
feedback: If the learner says 'adding a second bulb doesn't change the first one' (battery as constant-current source): add the second bulb live and show BOTH dim — the cell supplies a push, and the resulting current depends on the whole circuit.
If the learner conflates adding components with adding cells: place the two comparisons side by side and have them narrate each cause separately.
Affirm reasoning that keeps the two moves distinct and ties brightness to the share of push each bulb gets.
activities.rationale: Children must hold two opposite relationships simultaneously; an explicit side-by-side comparison isolates each cause (the working-scientifically steer) and is intended to prevent collapsing both into a single 'more parts = more light' rule.
sourceClaims: Y6 Electricity statutory requirement (verbatim): 'compare and give reasons for variations in how components function, including the brightness of bulbs, the loudness of buzzers and the on/off position of switches'; series only; change one component at a time.
learnerActions: Starting from a steady single-bulb circuit, add a second CELL in series, facing the same way as the first, and observe the bulb brighten.
Reset, then add a BULB in series and observe each bulb dim.
Use a side-by-side compare view (two circuits shown together) to hold both moves at once.
Sort or explain: which change increases brightness and which decreases it, and WHY — 'more cells push harder; more bulbs in series share the push between more components.'
Open a switch in the loop and observe the whole loop die; explain that an open switch breaks the complete path so nothing flows.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding cells and adding bulbs are opposite moves with different causes: more cells (in series) increase the push so bulbs brighten; more bulbs in series share the push so each dims. A switch simply completes or breaks the loop.

activities.title: Explain-it-back: challenge the reason and give evidence
feedback: If the learner only recites 'the current is shared' without distinguishing current from push: ask them to say what is equal everywhere (current) and what is split (the push/voltage).

For the parallel prediction: note that parallel bulbs each get (nearly) the full push of the cell and so are not dimmed the way series bulbs are — use it to test whether the reasoning transfers rather than as a recited fact.
Credit explanations that transfer the same reasoning to a buzzer's loudness or to the unscrewed-bulb case.
activities.rationale: A Socratic challenge probes whether the explanation is understood or merely recited, and the transfer prompts (parallel, unscrewing, order-swap, buzzer) test genuine coordination of current and energy-sharing. This is secondary to generating the comparison evidence first, and directly serves the statutory aim of giving reasons for variations.
sourceClaims: Y6 Electricity statutory requirement (verbatim): 'compare and give reasons for variations in how components function, including the brightness of bulbs, the loudness of buzzers and the on/off position of switches'; series only; change one component at a time.
The current-used-up/attenuation model (bulb nearest battery brightest) is a dominant misconception; series bulbs are equally bright because current is the same all the way round.
learnerActions: After a comparison, state out loud or in writing why the observed change happened.
Respond to a challenge such as 'your two bulbs are dim — why? are you sure the first isn't brighter?' and defend the answer with evidence from the circuit.

Answer probing extensions: If you unscrew the second bulb in a series pair, what happens to the first — and why? Does swapping the order (bulb-then-buzzer vs buzzer-then-bulb) change anything? Why does adding cells brighten but adding series bulbs dim?
Predict the PARALLEL case: two bulbs side by side (in parallel) compared with a single bulb, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: A reasoned explanation must coordinate two ideas — current is the same everywhere in a series loop, while the push (voltage) is shared between components — and this reasoning transfers to buzzers, to unscrewing a bulb, and to new configurations.

constraints: Keep everything qualitative at this stage: the main investigations use series circuits only (a parallel case appears only as an optional extension prediction), with no Ohm's law and no quantitative resistance.

Frame the KS2 reason as the cells' push being shared among more components. Flag that the precise mechanism (more components → more resistance → less current) is formalised at KS3, so loose 'energy used up' talk must not harden into 'current gets used up'.

Show that identical series bulbs are EQUALLY bright (not brighter nearer the battery) to confront the current-used-up idea directly; the current is the same all the way round the loop. Real bulbs may differ slightly because of manufacturing variation, not because of their position.

Recognition and multiple-choice compare items (e.g. 'which circuit's bulbs are brighter and why?', matching change→effect, sequencing circuits by brightness) can assess the reasoning and use reason distractors (current-used-up vs shared-push), but recognition-only responses do not elicit the learner's own change-and-compare that builds the explanation.
Tappable 'why?' flaps on annotated comparison circuits can serve as a reference for the reasons, but a reference cannot deliver the learner's own prediction-and-comparison.

A real bulbs-and-cells kit is a valuable complement; a screen simulation can render the equal-dimming current trace visible in a way a physical kit cannot easily show. Neither is claimed as the only way to teach this.

Optional feedback mechanisms that make the learning concrete: a per-bulb brightness gauge, a 'same current everywhere' highlight/band, live add/remove of bulbs and cells, a switch toggle, and a side-by-side compare mode. Offer these as supports, not mandatory requirements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source (IOP Spark / SPT electric circuits misconceptions) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the 'dominant misconception' and 'equally bright' claims as plausible but not independently confirmed here.

The qualitative KS2 framing of 'energy/push is shared' is a deliberate simplification; the source itself flags that the formal resistance/current account arrives at KS3. Ensure learners are not taught that current is literally consumed.

The original 2d-interactive entry asserts the equal-dimming reason 'is best made visible in the sim' over a real kit; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been softened to an affordance (a visible current trace), not a universal superiority claim.

The original 3d-interactive entry claimed a 3D model 'adds nothing'; this universal dismissal has been dropped. The underlying point retained is only that circuit behaviour and its reasons are not primarily spatial.

The 'clashing currents' misconception from the original pedagogy notes is addressed as feedback in the first activity via a single continuous-direction current trace, consistent with the current-is-equal-everywhere claim.

Independent review confirms the physics is coherent across summary, insights, actions and feedback: current is equal throughout a series loop, voltage/push is shared so series bulbs dim equally, cells added in series brighten, parallel bulbs receive the full push, and an open switch breaks the loop.

assess.poeTask: Build a series circuit with two identical bulbs and one cell. Before closing the switch, ask the child to predict whether the bulb nearer the battery will be brighter, dimmer, or the same as the far bulb — and why. The 'current used up first' idea predicts the near bulb is brighter; they glow equally. The committed reason exposes sequential reasoning, and reversing the cell afterwards confirms 'first' is not a real thing in the loop.
probeDeeper: Now put the two bulbs side by side (in parallel) instead. Predict each bulb's brightness compared with a single bulb on its own, and say why.
If you unscrew the second bulb in the series pair, what happens to the first one — and why?
Does it change anything if you swap the order — bulb then buzzer, versus buzzer then bulb?
Why does adding more cells make the bulbs brighter, but adding more bulbs in series makes them dimmer?
assess.correctAnswer: Both bulbs are equally bright. In a single series loop the current is the same through every component, so neither bulb gets 'more' first. Both are dimmer than a single bulb would be, because the cell's energy (voltage) is now shared between the two bulbs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sequential / local reasoning: 'the bulb nearest the battery is brighter because it gets the current first, before the other bulb takes its share'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the two bulbs glow equally, then reverse the battery to show it still doesn't matter which is 'first'; establish current is equal everywhere in a series loop.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bulb nearest the battery is brighter because it gets the current first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tier-1 answer ranks the near bulb brighter; Tier-2 has current being spent as it travels round the loop.

errorPatterns.pattern: More components means more brightness: 'two bulbs are brighter than one because there are more of them'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare one bulb to two in series directly; connect dimmer result to energy being shared, not multiplied. Revisit that brightness tracks the voltage each bulb gets.
errorPatterns.distractor: Both bulbs are brighter than a single bulb because there are more of them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts the series pair is brighter than a single bulb, treating 'more parts' as 'more of everything'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Battery as a constant-current source: 'the battery always pushes out the same current, so adding a second bulb doesn't change the first one'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the second bulb live and show BOTH dim; the battery supplies a voltage, and the current that results depends on the whole circuit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the first bulb's brightness is unaffected when a second bulb is added in series.

responseLevels.gap: Says the first component is brighter (current used up on the way), or that more bulbs means brighter.
responseLevels.full: Explains variations by coordinating current (the same throughout a series loop) with energy sharing (voltage split between components), predicts equal-but-dimmer series bulbs and full-brightness parallel bulbs, and gives reasons that transfer to buzzers and new configurations.
responseLevels.partial: Knows more bulbs in series are dimmer and that the current is 'shared', but recites it — cannot explain that the current is equal everywhere while the energy/voltage is shared, and cannot predict the parallel case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two identical bulbs are connected one after the other (in series) with a single cell. One child says the bulb nearest the battery will be brighter because it gets the current first. Are the two bulbs equally bright or not — and explain why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The sequential / 'current used up on the way' model predicts the first bulb is brighter. The correct model predicts equal brightness but both dimmer than one. A child cannot land on 'equal, and both dimmer than one, because the current is the same and the voltage is shared' without the right model, and the intuitive answer (first is brighter) is exactly what the misconception produces.
